edits.old: If creating an Atlas DNS override, scope the zone to the actual cluster-specific suffix, such as uzgh6.mongodb.net, rather than the entire mongodb.net namespace. Broad overrides can shadow unrelated public names and cause resolution failures. (high confidence)
edits.new: If creating a private DNS zone for an Atlas private endpoint in Azure, scope it to the cluster-specific subdomain (for example, <id>.mongodb.net, such as bzmphh.mongodb.net in one walkthrough) rather than the entire mongodb.net namespace. A zone for all of mongodb.net hijacks DNS resolution for all MongoDB Atlas clusters, so only the targeted cluster's traffic should go through the private endpoint. Sources: https://jaliyaudagedara.blogspot.com/2026/02/connecting-azure-to-mongodb-atlas-via.html?m=1

evidence.quote: Note that we use a specific subdomain (bzmphh.mongodb.net) rather than mongodb.net. This avoids hijacking DNS resolution for all MongoDB Atlas

edits.rationale: A third-party walkthrough (a blog, not MongoDB documentation) advises using the cluster-specific subdomain instead of mongodb.net to avoid hijacking DNS resolution for all Atlas clusters. The claim's 'resolution failures' wording and the 'shadow unrelated public names' wording are not stated in the source. uzgh6 is a cluster suffix used in MongoDB's Azure example, not in the blog.

edits.old: When diagnosing an Azure Atlas SRV connection, inspect the _mongodb._tcp seedlist and then resolve its returned target hostname. The expected combination is Atlas-assigned node ports and the endpoint NIC's private IP; checking only one A record misses service discovery. (medium confidence)
edits.new: When diagnosing an Azure Atlas SRV connection, look up the _mongodb._tcp SRV record to get the unique ports Atlas assigns per node and the target hostname, then resolve that hostname, which is a DNS A record that resolves to the private IP address of the private endpoint's network interface. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/security-private-endpoint.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/troubleshoot-private-endpoints.md

evidence.quote:
`1024`, `1025`, and `1026` are unique ports that

  Atlas assigns on the load balancer for each Atlas replica set node in the region for which you enabled Azure Private Link.
The hostname in the SRV record and the standard connection string is an DNS (Domain Name System) `A` record that resolves to the private IP address of the private endpoint's network interface.
Run `nslookup` with the `-type=SRV` flag to get the port numbers associated with each of the nodes in your cluster.

edits.rationale: MongoDB's docs show the SRV lookup returning Atlas-assigned unique ports and a pl-0 hostname, and say that hostname is an A record resolving to the endpoint NIC's private IP. The troubleshooting page suggests an SRV nslookup for ports. The assertion that checking only one A record misses service discovery is the claim's own inference, and no source states it, so it is dropped.
